back-rank-mate.name: back-rank mate
principles: Back-rank mate exploits a king trapped by its own shelter.
Back-rank mate threats grow when escape is limited by friendly blockers.
A back-rank mate plan turns restricted escape into forcing line pressure.

smothered-mate.name: smothered mate
principles: Smothered mate uses crowded defenders to take away escape squares.
Smothered mate threats can turn friendly shelter into a cage.
A smothered mate plan uses blocked escapes to make a check decisive.

anastasia-mate.name: Anastasia mate
principles: Anastasia mate combines an edge attack with covered escape squares.
Anastasia mate pressure grows when line threats meet restricted exits.
An Anastasia mate plan joins a clear edge line with control of escape.

arabian-mate.name: Arabian mate
principles: Arabian mate combines a line attack with control around a corner.
Arabian mate threats grow when coordinated attacks cover the remaining exits.
An Arabian mate plan uses mutual support to keep a cornered king trapped.

bodens-mate.name: Boden's mate
principles: Boden's mate uses crossing diagonal attacks to limit escape.
Boden's mate threats grow when diagonal pressure closes several exits together.
A Boden's mate plan joins two diagonals around a crowded king.

double-bishop-mate.name: double-bishop mate
principles: Double-bishop mate combines diagonal pressure against limited escape squares.
Double-bishop mate threats use separate diagonals to restrict different exits.
A double-bishop mate plan uses diagonal control to deny escape and defense.

dovetail-mate.name: dovetail mate
principles: Dovetail mate uses a king's own guards to close nearby escapes.
Dovetail mate threats turn nearby defenders into barriers to escape.
A dovetail mate plan combines a supported check with crowded escape squares.

hook-mate.name: hook mate
principles: Hook mate uses supported line attacks against a crowded king.
Hook mate threats grow when support and restricted escape work together.
A hook mate plan joins a protected checking point with control of escape.

french-defense.name: French Defense
principles: The French Defense often locks the center and shifts pressure to pawn chains.
French Defense tension can loosen the guards that hold a closed position together.
French Defense exchanges can open lines that a locked pawn chain had closed.

ruy-lopez.name: Ruy Lopez
principles: The Ruy Lopez builds pressure by challenging the support of key defenders.
Ruy Lopez pressure can turn a defender's extra duty into a tactical weakness.
In the Ruy Lopez, forcing threats can convert lasting pressure into material gains.

sicilian-defense.name: Sicilian Defense
principles: The Sicilian Defense creates uneven pawn structures that can open attacking chances.
Sicilian Defense imbalances can give active pieces targets that passive play would miss.
Sicilian Defense exchanges can open files toward exposed pieces.

caro-kann-defense.name: Caro-Kann Defense
principles: The Caro-Kann Defense supports a solid pawn chain that still needs active guards.
Caro-Kann Defense solidity depends on defenders staying active and connected.
In the Caro-Kann Defense, exchanges can expose pieces behind the pawn structure.

italian-game.name: Italian Game
principles: The Italian Game uses quick development to build pressure near the enemy king.
Italian Game activity can turn open lines into forcing threats.
An Italian Game attack can grow when development brings several pieces into play.

queens-gambit-declined.name: Queen's Gambit Declined
principles: The Queen's Gambit Declined keeps central tension while development adds pressure.
Queen's Gambit Declined tension can leave one guard responsible for several targets.
In the Queen's Gambit Declined, exchanges can change which pieces hold the center.

english-opening.name: English Opening
principles: The English Opening uses flexible pawn control to prepare pressure on weak squares.
English Opening flexibility can turn a change in structure into a new attack.
An English Opening plan uses control of key squares before committing to a break.

philidor-defense.name: Philidor Defense
principles: The Philidor Defense holds a compact center but can leave pieces short of room.
Philidor Defense pieces need active squares so compact shelter does not become a trap.
In the Philidor Defense, exchanges can free cramped pieces or expose their guards.

scandinavian-defense.name: Scandinavian Defense
principles: The Scandinavian Defense opens the center early and makes active development important.
Scandinavian Defense development can punish a piece that advances without enough support.
In the Scandinavian Defense, open central lines can make loose pieces important targets.

scotch-game.name: Scotch Game
principles: The Scotch Game opens central lines and rewards quick development.
Scotch Game activity can exploit a loose defender on an open line.
In the Scotch Game, central exchanges can reveal targets before development is finished.

modern-defense.name: Modern Defense
principles: The Modern Defense lets opposing pawns advance before challenging their support.
Modern Defense counterplay can turn a large structure into a target.
Modern Defense breaks can release cramped pieces while attacking the opposing center.

four-knights-defense.name: Four Knights Defense
principles: The Four Knights Defense develops medium pieces quickly to contest useful squares.
Four Knights Defense development can expose targets when active pieces lose support.
In the Four Knights Defense, coordination helps convert development into threats.

kings-gambit-accepted.name: King's Gambit Accepted
principles: The King's Gambit Accepted trades a pawn for open lines and faster development.
King's Gambit Accepted positions balance extra material against faster attacking play.
In the King's Gambit Accepted, active development can matter more than keeping a pawn.

pirc-defense.name: Pirc Defense
principles: The Pirc Defense allows a broad pawn center before seeking counterplay against it.
Pirc Defense counterplay can challenge the support of an advancing structure.
In the Pirc Defense, active counterplay can reveal targets left by a broad center.

damiano-defense.name: Damiano Defense
principles: The Damiano Defense weakens king shelter when early pawn moves delay development.
Damiano Defense weaknesses can let forcing threats outrun slower development.
In the Damiano Defense, weak diagonals can make king safety more urgent than material.

rapport-jobava-system.name: Rapport-Jobava System
principles: The Rapport-Jobava System uses fast development to pressure unstable defenses.
Rapport-Jobava System coordination can turn an active post into a forcing threat.
In the Rapport-Jobava System, coordinated pieces can exploit loose guards before they regroup.

vienna-game.name: Vienna Game
principles: The Vienna Game combines development with pawn support for an early attack.
Vienna Game activity can make weak guards important before development is finished.
In the Vienna Game, coordinated development can turn control of key squares into threats.

zugzwang.name: zugzwang
principles: Zugzwang makes the need to move a weakness when every choice loses ground.
In zugzwang, a waiting step can make the defender break a useful restriction.
Zugzwang plans preserve useful restrictions until the opponent must give one up.

pawn-endgame.name: pawn endgame
principles: A pawn endgame rewards king activity and careful timing in the race to promote.
Pawn endgame timing can turn one spare turn into a lasting advantage.
In a pawn endgame, winning a tempo can change who reaches a key square.

queen-endgame.name: queen endgame
principles: A queen endgame rewards active threats that give the opposing king little rest.
Queen endgame threats can force defense before a passed piece can be stopped.
In a queen endgame, a checking threat can outweigh a small material edge.

queen-rook-endgame.name: queen-rook endgame
principles: A queen-rook endgame rewards coordinated threats along open lines.
Queen-rook endgame coordination can stretch a defense across several lines.
In a queen-rook endgame, active checks can matter more than passive shelter.

advanced-pawn.name: advanced pawn
principles: An advanced pawn can tie down defenders by threatening promotion.
An advanced-pawn threat can divert guards from other targets.
An advanced pawn can create threats while defenders worry about its promotion.

knight-endgame.name: knight endgame
principles: A knight endgame needs coordinated king and pawn support against distant threats.
Knight endgame targets can be hard to save when short-range defenders are separated.
In a knight endgame, a spare tempo can decide whether a passer is stopped.

pin.name: pin
principles: A pin can tie a defender to something more valuable behind it.
A pin can make a guard unable to help with another threat.
Pin pressure can make a defender choose between losing its guard duty and material.

fork.name: fork
principles: A fork can threaten two targets at once.
A fork can leave too little time to protect both targets.
A fork gains force when saving one target leaves the other exposed.

discovered-attack.name: discovered attack
principles: A discovered attack reveals pressure by moving a blocker out of the way.
A discovered attack can release one threat while the moving blocker creates another.
Discovered attack plans use the blocker and the hidden attacker for separate duties.

skewer.name: skewer
principles: A skewer attacks a valuable target while another waits on the same line.
A skewer can expose the next target when the first must move away.
Skewer pressure uses a forcing threat to uncover material along a shared line.

double-check.name: double check
principles: Double check combines two attacks in the same turn.
Double check cannot be answered by stopping only one of the attacks.
A double check leaves a king needing an escape rather than a single block.

attraction.name: attraction
principles: Attraction can draw a piece onto a square where it becomes vulnerable.
Attraction can use an offered target to draw a defender into a new attack.
An attraction plan changes a defender's square so a later threat can reach it.

x-ray-attack.name: x-ray attack
principles: An x-ray attack keeps pressure on a target through an intervening piece.
An x-ray attack can grow stronger when a blocker leaves its line.
X-ray attack pressure can survive an exchange because another attacker remains on the line.

deflection.name: deflection
principles: Deflection can draw a guard away from something it needs to protect.
Deflection can make one defender abandon a duty to meet a new threat.
A deflection plan uses competing duties to loosen the protection of a target.

hanging-piece.name: hanging piece
principles: A hanging piece has too little protection and can become a tactical target.
A hanging piece can be lost when its side must answer another threat.
Hanging piece tactics compare the target's protection with the cost of taking it.

sacrifice.name: sacrifice
principles: A sacrifice can trade material for time, open lines, or a stronger attack.
A sacrifice can make a defender change its duties before the attack continues.
A sacrifice is useful when the resulting threats outweigh the material given up.

interference.name: interference
principles: Interference can weaken a defense by blocking the link between its pieces.
Interference can cut a guard's line without capturing the guard itself.
An interference plan separates a target from the piece that supports it.

trapped-piece.name: trapped piece
principles: A trapped piece can be lost when its safe escape squares disappear.
A trapped piece becomes easier to attack when its retreats are restricted.
Trapped piece tactics combine pressure on the target with control of its exits.

capturing-defender.name: capturing the defender
principles: Capturing the defender can leave its target without enough protection.
Capturing the defender can weaken a target before that target is attacked directly.
Capturing the defender changes the support available to the pieces it guarded.

clearance.name: clearance
principles: Clearance can improve an attack by removing a blocker from a useful line.
Clearance can free a route while the moving piece creates a separate threat.
A clearance plan makes a line available to an attacker that could not use it before.

intermezzo.name: intermezzo
principles: An intermezzo inserts an urgent threat before the expected reply.
An intermezzo can gain time by making a new threat more urgent than a recapture.
An intermezzo changes the order of play so a forcing threat is handled first.

en-passant.name: en passant
principles: En passant allows a passing capture immediately after a two-square pawn advance.
En passant rights disappear if another reply is chosen first.
En passant can remove a neighboring pawn and change an important attack line.

under-promotion.name: under-promotion
principles: Under-promotion can create a useful attack without choosing the most valuable piece.
Under-promotion changes the available threats rather than simply maximizing material value.
Under-promotion can avoid stalemate or create an attack that a different choice would miss.

castling.name: castling
principles: Castling can improve king shelter while bringing a corner piece into play.
Castling combines safer shelter with activity from a second piece.
Castling can connect a safety plan with pressure along a newly useful line.
